objectives: Describe the properties of alpha, beta and gamma radiation

questions.q: Why do some atoms undergo nuclear decay?
questions.a: Their nucleus is unstable (an unbalanced number of protons and neutrons), so it releases radiation to become more stable.

questions.q: What does the term half-life mean?
questions.a: The time taken for the number of unstable nuclei, or the activity, to fall to half of its starting value.
questions.hint: The time for the number of unstable ______ to fall by ______.

questions.q: Name the three types of nuclear radiation and put them in order of ionising power, from most to least.
questions.a: Alpha (most ionising), beta, then gamma (least ionising).

questions.q: The half-life of Zn-71 is 2.4 minutes. You start with 100.0 g. How much is left after 7.2 minutes?
What is meant by the activity of a source, and what unit is it measured in?
questions.a: Activity is the number of nuclear decays per second. It is measured in becquerel (Bq).

build.instruction: These statements are incorrect. Rewrite each one so it is right.

statements.text: Once youve had an X-ray you stay radioactive and can give off radiation to other people.
statements.correction: An X-ray irradiates you, it does not make you radioactive. You do not give off radiation afterwards.

statements.text: Irradiated food is dangerous because the food itself becomes radioactive.
statements.correction: Irradiated food does not become radioactive. The radiation kills bacteria but leaves no radioactivity behind, so it is safe.

statements.text: Gamma sources always do the most damage inside the body because they travel furthest.
statements.correction: Inside the body an alpha source does the most damage because it is the most strongly ionising.

statements.text: Contamination and irradiation are just two words for the same thing.
statements.correction: Irradiation is being exposed to radiation. Contamination is having radioactive material on or inside you.

build.q: Which of these is an example of contamination rather than irradiation?
options: Standing near a sealed gamma source
Food being sterilised with gamma rays
build.explanation: Breathing in radon puts radioactive material inside the body, which then gives off radiation. The others expose the person to radiation from an outside source.
build.commonError: Choosing the X-ray because it feels dangerous, but an X-ray only irradiates you.

developing.q: Define the terms irradiation and contamination.
developing.a: Irradiation: an object or person is exposed to radiation but does not become radioactive. Contamination: radioactive material is put on or inside an object or person, which then gives off radiation.

developing.q: Give one everyday example of irradiation and one of contamination.
developing.a: Irradiation: an X-ray, or food sterilised with gamma rays. Contamination: breathing in radon gas, or radioactive dust landing on the skin.

reaching.q: A source has an activity of 800 Bq and a half-life of 6 hours. What is its activity after 18 hours?
reaching.given: activity = 800 Bq, half-life = 6 hours, time = 18 hours

reaching.q: Explain why beta and gamma are more dangerous than alpha outside the body, but alpha is most dangerous inside the body.
reaching.a: Outside: alpha is stopped by skin and clothing so it cannot reach living cells, while beta and gamma pass through and reach organs. Inside: alpha is the most strongly ionising, so it does the most damage to nearby cells.

mastering.q: A hospital needs a radioactive source to use as a medical tracer inside a patient. Evaluate the properties the source should have, and explain the risks and benefits.
mastering.a: A tracer is swallowed or injected, so it is a source of contamination inside the body. A gamma emitter is best because gamma can pass out of the body to be detected, while alpha or beta would be absorbed and damage cells without escaping. The half-life should be short so the activity falls quickly and exposure is limited, but long enough to finish the scan. Risk: the radioactive material can spread to healthy tissue and ionise cells, which can cause cancer. Benefit: imaging with a tracer can replace some invasive surgery.

indicativeContent.text: A tracer is swallowed or injected, so it is contamination inside the body
A gamma emitter is best because gamma can pass out of the body to be detected
Alpha or beta would be absorbed inside the body and would not be detected
A short half-life limits how long the patient is exposed
The half-life must still be long enough to complete the scan
Risk: the material can ionise healthy cells and cause cancer
Benefit: imaging can replace some invasive surgery

objectives: Define specific latent heat, and the difference between fusion and vaporisation

questions.q: What is the difference between irradiation and contamination?
questions.a: Irradiation: exposed to radiation but you do not become radioactive. Contamination: radioactive material is on or inside you, so you give off radiation.

questions.q: Give one advantage of using irradiation.
questions.a: It sterilises food or equipment without high temperatures, or it can kill cancer cells, or check the thickness of materials.

questions.q: In a heating experiment, name the independent variable and the dependent variable.
questions.a: Independent: the energy supplied (or time heated). Dependent: the mass of water boiled away.

questions.q: Why should a measurement be repeated and a mean taken?
questions.a: To reduce the effect of random error and make the result more reliable.

questions.q: A student measures a value that is larger than the true value. Suggest one reason why.
questions.a: Some energy is lost to the surroundings instead of boiling the water, so more energy seems to be needed per kilogram.

engage.hook: Would you rather be boiled alive in water or in olive oil, or would it make no difference?
engage.content: Olive oil boils at about 300 C, water at 100 C. No matter how long you heat liquid water, it will not go above 100 C. Where does all the extra energy go?
engage.imageDescription: old painting of people boiling something in a large cauldron over a fire

learn.heading: Key words: latent heat, fusion, vaporisation

definitions.definition: The energy needed to change the state of one kilogram of a substance without changing its temperature. It is measured in joules per kilogram (J/kg).
The energy needed to melt one kilogram of a solid into a liquid without changing its temperature.
The energy needed to boil one kilogram of a liquid into a gas without changing its temperature.

learn.heading: The latent heat equation
learn.example: To boil away 0.10 kg of water needs E = m x L = 0.10 x 2,260,000 = 226,000 J.

learn.heading: Heating curve for water

features.label: Rising sections
features.description: The temperature rises as the solid, liquid or gas is heated.

features.label: Flat section at 0 C
features.description: Energy is melting the ice. The temperature stays the same (latent heat of fusion).

features.label: Flat section at 100 C
features.description: Energy is boiling the water. The temperature stays the same (latent heat of vaporisation).

learn.instruction: Sketch the heating curve and label where latent heat is being supplied.
learn.imageDescription: heating curve graph of temperature against energy for water showing two flat plateaus where the ice melts and where the water boils

build.intro: Measure the specific latent heat of vaporisation of water by finding how much energy is needed to boil away a measured mass of water.
steps: Set up the immersion heater in a beaker of water, connected to the power pack through the joulemeter.
Place the beaker on the weighing scales and record the starting mass.
Reset the joulemeter to zero and switch on. Let the water boil steadily.
After a few minutes, switch off and record the energy on the joulemeter and the new mass.
The mass lost is the mass of water boiled away. Work out L = energy supplied / mass boiled away.
build.warning: Steam and boiling water cause severe burns. Keep hands clear and switch off before touching the beaker.
build.imageDescription: apparatus diagram immersion heater beaker of boiling water on a balance to measure latent heat

questions.q: Why does the water stay at 100 C while it boils, even though energy is still being supplied?
questions.a: The energy is being used to change state (break the bonds between water molecules), not to raise the temperature.

questions.q: Why is the measured value of L usually larger than the true value?
questions.a: Some energy is lost to the surroundings, so more energy is recorded than is actually used to boil the water.

questions.q: 180,000 J of energy boils away 0.080 kg of water. Find L.
How much energy is needed to boil away 0.25 kg of water? (L = 2,260,000 J/kg)

developing.q: What is meant by the specific latent heat of vaporisation of water?
developing.a: The energy needed to boil one kilogram of water into steam without changing its temperature.

developing.q: State the equation that links energy, mass and specific latent heat, and give the unit of each quantity.
developing.a: E = m L. E in joules (J), m in kilograms (kg), L in joules per kilogram (J/kg).

reaching.q: In an experiment, 240,000 J of energy boiled away 0.106 kg of water. Calculate the specific latent heat and the percentage difference from the true value of 2,260,000 J/kg.
reaching.solve: L = 2,264,000 J/kg, about 0.2% from the true value

mastering.q: Write up this experiment to measure the specific latent heat of water. Include the aim, method, a safety precaution, your result, and an evaluation of why the value is not exact. (6 marks)
mastering.a: Aim: to measure the specific latent heat of vaporisation of water. Method: boil water with an immersion heater through a joulemeter, record the energy supplied and the mass of water boiled away, then use L = E / m. Safety: steam causes burns, so switch off before touching the beaker. Result: a value close to 2,260,000 J/kg. Evaluation: the measured value is a little too high because some energy is lost to the surroundings rather than boiling the water. Repeating and taking a mean, and insulating the beaker, would improve it.

indicativeContent.text: Aim: to measure the specific latent heat of vaporisation of water
Method: boil water with an immersion heater through a joulemeter
Record the energy supplied and the mass of water boiled away
Use L = E / m to calculate the specific latent heat
Safety: steam and boiling water cause burns
Evaluation: energy is lost to the surroundings, so the value is too high
Improve by insulating the beaker and repeating to take a mean

referenceData.note: Energy supplied plotted against mass of water boiled away. The gradient of the line is the specific latent heat of vaporisation.

objectives: State what a solar eclipse is

questions.q: Explain why we have day and night.
questions.a: The Earth spins on its axis once every 24 hours. The side facing the Sun has day, the side facing away has night.

questions.q: Explain why we have a year.
questions.a: The Earth orbits the Sun. One full orbit takes 365.25 days, which is one year.

questions.q: Why does the Moon appear to have phases?
questions.a: The Moon orbits the Earth and reflects sunlight. We see different amounts of the lit side as it moves, which gives the phases.

questions.q: What is the name of the Moon phase when we cannot see any of it lit up?
questions.a: A new moon.

questions.q: What does the Moon orbit?
questions.a: The Earth.

developing.q: Fill in the gaps: In a solar eclipse the _____ moves between the _____ and the Earth. The dark middle of the shadow is the _____.
Draw and label a solar eclipse. Label the Sun, the Moon, the Earth, the umbra and the penumbra.
developing.a: Sun, then Moon, then Earth in a line. Umbra is the dark central shadow, penumbra is the lighter outer shadow.

reaching.q: Write a short paragraph explaining the difference between a solar eclipse and a lunar eclipse.
reaching.a: In a solar eclipse the Moon is between the Sun and the Earth, so the Moon's shadow falls on the Earth and the Sun appears to go dark. In a lunar eclipse the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, so the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon and the Moon can look red.

mastering.q: Compare a solar and a lunar eclipse. Give 3 similarities, 3 features unique to solar eclipses, and 3 unique to lunar eclipses.
mastering.a: Similarities: both need the Sun, Earth and Moon in a line; both involve a shadow; both are rare. Solar only: Moon between Sun and Earth, shadow on Earth, happens at new moon. Lunar only: Earth between Sun and Moon, shadow on Moon, Moon looks red, happens at full moon.

indicativeContent.text: Similarity: both need the Sun, Earth and Moon nearly in a line
Similarity: both involve one body casting a shadow
Similarity: both are rare because the Moon's orbit is tilted
Solar only: the Moon is between the Sun and the Earth
Solar only: the Moon's shadow falls on the Earth and it happens at a new moon
Lunar only: the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon
Lunar only: the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon, which looks red, at a full moon

engage.content: Long ago, nobody knew why the Sun suddenly went dark in the day. Some thought a dragon was eating it. Today we can predict eclipses to the minute, and even use them to make discoveries.

learn.heading: Ancient times: eclipses as omens

items: Ancient China and Babylon recorded eclipses
In one Chinese story, a dragon was eating the Sun, and people banged drums to scare it away
Babylonian astronomers spotted that eclipses repeat in a pattern of about 18 years

learn.imageDescription: ancient Chinese illustration of a dragon eating the Sun during an eclipse

learn.heading: 585 BC: the eclipse that stopped a battle

items: The Greek writer Herodotus tells the story of a solar eclipse during a battle between the Medes and the Lydians
The soldiers were so frightened that the day turned to night that they stopped fighting and made peace
The Greek thinker Thales is said to have predicted it, though historians are not sure how

learn.imageDescription: ancient painting of two armies stopping a battle as a solar eclipse darkens the sky

learn.heading: 1715: Halley predicts the path

items: The English scientist Edmond Halley predicted the exact path of a total eclipse across England in 1715
He drew a map showing where and when the shadow would fall
This showed eclipses follow the laws of physics, not magic or omens

learn.imageDescription: Edmond Halley 1715 eclipse map showing the path of the Moon's shadow across England

learn.heading: 1868: a new element found in the Sun

items: During a total eclipse in 1868, the scientist Janssen studied the light from the Sun
He saw a yellow line that did not match any element known on Earth
It was a brand new element, named helium after Helios, the Greek Sun god
Helium is the only element discovered in space before it was found on Earth

learn.imageDescription: spectroscope splitting sunlight into a spectrum with a bright yellow helium line

learn.heading: 1919: proving Einstein right

items: During a total eclipse in 1919, the scientist Eddington photographed stars near the dark Sun
The starlight had been bent by the Sun's gravity, exactly as Einstein predicted
This eclipse proved Einstein's theory of general relativity and made him world famous

developing.a: 585 BC: an eclipse is said to have stopped a battle (Thales). 1715: Halley predicted the eclipse path. 1868: helium found in the Sun. 1919: Eddington proved Einstein's gravity.

developing.q: Why were ancient people frightened of eclipses?
developing.a: They did not know why the Sun suddenly went dark in the day, so they thought it was a bad omen or a creature eating the Sun.

reaching.q: Explain how the 1868 eclipse led to the discovery of a new element.
reaching.a: During the eclipse, scientists studied the light from the Sun and saw a yellow line that did not match any known element. This was a new element, helium, the first element found in space before it was found on Earth.

mastering.q: Explain how our understanding of eclipses has changed from ancient times to today, using examples.
mastering.a: In ancient times people feared eclipses as omens, such as a dragon eating the Sun, and a 585 BC eclipse is said to have stopped a battle. Over time scientists learned that eclipses follow the laws of physics: Halley predicted the path of the 1715 eclipse, helium was discovered in the Sun in 1868, and in 1919 an eclipse proved Einstein's theory of gravity. Today we predict eclipses exactly and use them to study the Sun.
